title: Last Car in the Garage
story: A small parking garage logs a car's ticket number twice, once when the car drives in and once when it drives out. The log is one long list in no useful order.
At closing time exactly one car is still inside, so exactly one ticket appears only once. The gate computer can read the log once but has almost no spare memory.
task: Write carStillInside(log). Every ticket number in log appears exactly twice, except one that appears exactly once. Return that number.
Aim for one pass and O(1) extra memory: no map, no set, no sorted copy.
constraints: Exactly one number appears once. Every other number appears exactly twice.

examples.explanation: Cars 512 and 87 both came in and went out, so each appears twice. Ticket 340 appears only once, so that car is still inside.
The two 4s are neighbours, but the two 9s are not, so you cannot assume that matching tickets sit together. The ticket that appears once is 2.

hints: What is x XOR x for any number x? And x XOR 0?
XOR of a number with itself is 0, and XOR with 0 changes nothing. XOR also ignores order: a ^ b ^ a equals a ^ a ^ b.
So what if you XOR every ticket in the log together? Each pair cancels, wherever its halves sit. What is left?
Start with result = 0 and XOR in every number. The pairs cancel, and the one ticket with no partner is left.
bruteForce: Counting tickets in a hash map takes O(n) time but stores up to n / 2 numbers, which the gate computer cannot afford. Checking each ticket against every other one uses no extra memory but costs O(n²), which is about 900 million comparisons for 30,001 entries.
Sorting the log and then comparing neighbours in steps of two uses little memory, but it costs O(n log n) and needs a sortable copy or permission to reorder the log.

js: * @param {number[]} log  every ticket twice except one

tests.note: the answer is 0 and sits at the start
the answer is at the very end
pairs are not next to each other
1 ^ 2 = 3: summing or OR-ing the distinct values would be wrong
the lone ticket is 0, in the middle: a "found yet?" check on the value 0 breaks

js: result ^= ticket; // pairs cancel: x ^ x = 0
py: result ^= ticket  # pairs cancel: x ^ x = 0
walkthrough: XOR compares two numbers bit by bit and gives 1 where the bits differ. Two facts do the work: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x. Order does not matter, so every pair cancels however far apart its halves are.
• 11 ^ 9 = 1011 ^ 1001 = 0010 (2). The 9 cancels too, so the answer is 2.
The middle values 13 and 11 look meaningless, but only the final value matters.
solution.timeWhy: The loop does one XOR for each log entry.
solution.spaceWhy: The only extra storage is a single running value.
solution.takeaway: XOR cancels any value that appears an even number of times. You can use it to find the one unpaired value among pairs, or to find a difference, without extra memory.
